title: How inflation changes how much your wages are worth

breadcrumb.text: How inflation changes how much your wages are worth

body.text: 26 June 2017
Workers have started to feel the squeeze in their finances, after wage growth recently fell below inflation for the first time since 2014.
In April 2017, inflation rose to 2.6% year-on-year, while three-month average wage growth was 2.1% over the same time period.
At the same time last year, wage growth was similar (2.2%) but workers enjoyed the benefits of a low rate of inflation (0.7%).

body.text: The recent increase in inflation is, in part, due to a fall in the value of sterling after the EU referendum, but the fall in wage growth is unusual as it occurs at a time when employment is at a record high. A high employment rate is an indicator of a strong economy, and wage growth is usually expected.

body.text: It is important to note that inflation affects everyone differently - even employees who have the exact same wage growth - as it depends on what items you buy and whether those prices have risen or gone down.

body.h3: Private and public sector employees experience different pay changes
body.text: Private and public sector employees experience different pay changes

body.h3: Private and public sector employees experience different pay changes
body.text: While workers across nearly all industries are experiencing pay growth beneath inflation levels, it differs between industries and sectors.

body.h3: Private and public sector employees experience different pay changes
body.text: The private sector is experiencing pay growth at a higher level than the public sector (2.3% and 1.1% respectively). This means public sector workers are likely to be more affected, on average, as inflation rises.

body.h3: Private and public sector employees experience different pay changes
body.text: To illustrate this, you can look at the fictional examples of Ali and Becca.

body.h3: Private and public sector employees experience different pay changes
body.text: Ali is in the public sector, and Becca is in the private sector. body.h3: What will the future bring?
body.text: What will the future bring?

body.h3: What will the future bring?
body.text: It’s impossible to predict with certainty what will happen to pay growth in the future, but the Office for Budget Responsibility have forecast that real earnings will not have returned to pre-downturn levels by 2020 to 21, despite record employment and a more skilled workforce.

body.h3: What will the future bring?
body.text: Note: Pay growth can be affected by a number of factors other than pay rises. The wage growth figures in this article are from the average weekly earnings (AWE) series, which takes into account money paid to employees before tax and other deductions. The estimates also reflect changes in the mix of high and low earning jobs in the economy, bonuses, changes in the number of paid hours worked and the impact of employees paid at different rates joining and leaving individual businesses. The estimates do not include earnings of self-employed people.
